Text: {{c1::Just culture}} is an approach to leadership in organizations that balances {{c2::fairness}} and {{c2::accountability}} and encourages people to {{c3::report errors and near misses}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: accountability is not only individual — in a just culture, both the EMS system and the individual provider are held accountable for overall safety.

Why: the focus is risk management — proactively identifying problems in the system that could lead to error or opportunities to improve safety.

Mechanism: behaviors associated with error or risk are categorized as human error, at-risk behavior, or reckless behavior.

Text: The {{c1::continuum of care}} is the concept of health care providers working as a unified team from {{c2::first patient contact}} to {{c2::patient discharge}}, improving performance, safety, and ultimately {{c3::patient outcomes}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: in the older model of emergency care, providers worked independently and passed the patient from one individual or group to the next.

Ex: community paramedicine and mobile integrated healthcare (MIH) teams may be the best examples of the continuum-of-care team concept.

Text: In EMS, a {{c1::group::group/team}} consists of providers working {{c2::independently::independently/interdependently}} to help the patient, whereas a {{c1::team::group/team}} consists of providers who are {{c2::assigned specific roles}} and work {{c2::interdependently::independently/interdependently}}, in a coordinated manner, under a {{c2::designated leader}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: providers merely gathered together on an emergency call are not automatically a true team.

Ex: the triage, treatment, and transport groups at a mass-casualty incident are classic EMS groups (each unit working independently).

Distinguish: NIMS uses the word group more narrowly (an organizational level dividing an incident by function, often across geographic boundaries); the group-vs-team contrast uses the general sense.
